idiom_name: enum state + exhaustive match decider + serde-persisted row + tokio timeout
implementation_notes: Rust makes the decider cheap and honest: states are enum variants, transitions an exhaustive match, and a forgotten variant does not compile; the instance is a serialised struct (serde) in a database row and tokio::time::timeout bounds in-process waits. What the language does not supply is durability or correlation - the outbox write, the deadline sweep and the compensating steps are hand-written - so a hand-rolled enum machine is the usual shape until a durable-execution runtime is adopted. The classic state-object form is still justified when each state carries substantial behaviour and per-state modules read better than one growing match arm.
pitfalls: A serde representation that is not explicitly tagged and versioned breaks every running instance when a variant gains a field; derive with a stable tag and keep a version marker in the row.
tokio::time::timeout cancels the future but not the side effect already triggered on the remote side, so activities still need idempotency keys.

Holding a tokio Mutex across an await while another message for the same instance arrives serialises the wrong thing and can deadlock; serialise per instance (actor task or row lock) instead of relying on one global lock.
Recovering an instance by deserialising into the current enum silently loses states that were deleted - keep old variants until no instance uses them.
